text: Well now. I drove to Bright River for a boy, and there she was, sitting on a pile of shingles with a carpetbag. She talked the whole way home. I didn’t mind. I liked it. When you pick your picture, look at what she noticed that day. A girl who calls a plain old road the White Way of Delight… well now. That tells you something about her.

I had Anne in my class for two years, and I can tell you she didn’t change all at once. Nobody does. She changed in moments: a mistake, a quarrel, a kindness she didn’t expect. A real turning point has a before and an after. Look for the place where she stops and becomes a little different. You’ll know it when you find it.

Oh, I could pick so many! The raspberry cordial, when Mother wouldn’t let me see her. Or the night Minnie May had croup and Anne knew exactly what to do. Mother forgave everything after that. Anne was so brave, and she never once bragged about it. Whatever you choose, pick an ink that matches how she felt. Anne would say that’s the most romantic part.

I’ll own up. One of Anne’s turning points was me, calling her Carrots. She cracked a slate over my head, and she wouldn’t speak to me for years. Then one evening she stopped me on the road and held out her hand. If you pick the slate, go easy on me. If you don’t, find something that shows how she got from that slate to that road.

She gave up the Avery to stay with me. I told her I couldn’t let her sacrifice herself, and she laughed and said there was no sacrifice. That’s Anne for you. Now, don’t just tell me she grew up. Anybody can say that. Put the girl at Bright River beside the girl at the gate and let them speak for themselves. Well. There it is.

I’ve lived in Avonlea all my life, and there isn’t a road or a pond I couldn’t name for you. That child put new names on half of them. The Lake of Shining Waters! It’s Barry’s pond, and always was. Still, I’ll grant you, she saw things in this place. Put your pins where things happened to her. I’d have done it in half the time, mind.

Oh, a cover! It’s the most important page, because it’s the one everybody sees first, so it ought to say something true. When I was little I thought growing up meant everything turning grand. It doesn’t. You get pruned down and branched out. Write your sentence so it’s true for anyone, not only me. That’s the hard part. It’s also the best part.
